newsitem.title: USA: U.S. orders Americans out of Albania.
newsitem.headline: U.S. orders Americans out of Albania.

text.p: The United States on Wednesday ordered 160 U.S. government employees and their dependents to leave Albania because of worsening instability.

An estimated 2,000 other Americans living in Albania were also urged to leave the country. Officials said Americans would leave by commercial or charter air flights and there would be no need for U.S. military evacuation assistance.

State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said U.S. fears about the Albanian crisis had grown because insurgents have not accepted a peace proposal put forward by President Sali Berisha and because large numbers of armed civilians have broken into caches, stealing weapons and creating a highly volatile situation.

"In the view of the concerns we have about the security situation in Albania, we are ordering a drawdown of non-essential United States government personnel in Albania ... Dependents and non-essential personnel will depart Albania in the coming days," he said.
In addition, "we are advising American citizens to consider departing Albania as soon as possible," he said.
Burns said the United States welcomed Berisha's appointment of a new prime minister, Bashkim Fino, a Socialist, and expected more new government appointments later in the day.

"We urge all Albanian citizens to support this government and to work for a political, non-violent resolution to the current crisis," he said. He exhorted insurgents to "lay down their arms and to understand the fact that the opposition is now part of the government."

He also called on "the new government and all opposition forces to establish a decent political dialogue that will lead to a cessation of hostilities and that might restore the peace so that the economic problems that stimulated this crisis in the first place can be attended to."

To this end, Burns noted the crisis is already causing problems for Albania because the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank "want to send a mission there but cannot do so because of the current instability."
There are "roughly 2,000" private American citizens in Albania, Burns said.

The 160 U.S. employees and their dependents include 74 Peace Corps volunteers, 39 State Department employees and dependents, 54 U.S. Agency for International Development contractors and their dependents. The rest are U.S. Information Agency-related individuals and Fulbright scholars.
U.S. Ambassador Marisa Lino and 17 other diplomats will remain in Tirana, Burns said.

Fino, the new prime minister, said on Wednesday he wanted talks with armed rebels holding towns in southern Albania. In some areas, the rebellion seemed to have deteriorated into lawlessness, with armed gangs roaming at will through rebel-held towns, robbing motorists, terrorising women and shooting at travelers from Greece.

Anti-government rebels pillaged an arms depot near the town of Elbasan, a mere 34 miles (55 km) from Tirana. In the capital itself, eyewitnesses reported groups of men had entered the military academy and removed small arms.

As rebellion moved nearer the capital, Fino met political parties to discuss forming an interim government to oversee new elections. The weekend deal between Berisha and the opposition called for an interim all-party government, new elections by June and an amnesty for rebels to hand in thousands of weapons looted from army barracks.
